cards.front: What is the particle model of matter, and what is it used for?
cards.back: All matter is made of tiny **particles**. The model describes where particles are and how they move, which explains observable properties even though particles are too small to see.
cards.hint: Think about what the model explains, not what it looks like.

cards.front: How do particles differ in solids, liquids and gases?
cards.back: In a **solid**, particles are close together in fixed positions and vibrate. In a **liquid**, they stay close but move past one another. In a **gas**, they are far apart and move freely in different directions.
cards.hint: Compare the spacing and how freely the particles move.

cards.back: **Diffusion** is the net spreading of particles from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration, caused by random movement.
cards.hint: Think about dye spreading through still water.

cards.back: A **molecule** is a group of atoms held together by chemical bonds. For example, an oxygen molecule contains two oxygen atoms.
An **atom** is the smallest unit of an element that retains its chemical identity.

cards.front: Why do tiny visible particles suspended in water move irregularly?
cards.back: **Brownian motion**: unseen water molecules strike the visible particles unevenly from different sides, so the particles change direction irregularly.
cards.hint: Think about what is actually seen and what is not.

cards.front: Does diffusion mean every particle moves from high to low concentration?
cards.back: No. Particles move **randomly** in every direction. Only the overall net spread goes from higher to lower concentration.
cards.hint: Consider what the word net means.

cards.front: Are the water molecules seen in Brownian motion?
cards.back: No. Only the larger suspended particles are seen. Their irregular movement is evidence of collisions with the unseen water molecules.
cards.hint: Separate the visible particles from the fluid particles.

cards.front: Does every substance consist of separate molecules?
cards.back: No. Some substances contain atoms in **extended structures** instead of discrete molecules.

cards.front: What changes, and what stays the same, when a substance melts?
cards.back: Its particles leave fixed positions and can move past one another. The particles stay the same; only their arrangement, movement and spacing change.
cards.hint: Particles do not turn into different particles.

cards.front: Why do solids keep their shape but liquids flow?
cards.back: Solid particles are held in fixed positions, so the shape is kept. Liquid particles can move past one another, so the substance flows.
cards.hint: Link the particle movement to the observable behaviour.

cards.front: Why does a gas released in one part of a room spread throughout the room?
cards.back: Its particles move freely and randomly, colliding and travelling in every direction. This **diffusion** spreads them through the room without any stirring.
cards.hint: Apply the idea of random movement to a gas.
